newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers vow disruption, PM rejects demands.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers vow disruption, PM rejects demands.

text.p: Greece's defiant farmers vowed on Thursday to step up their 22-day national road blockade after Prime Minister Costas Simitis said he would quit before giving in to their demands.
Thousands of farmers left their barricades and descended on Athens in coaches on Thursday to march on parliament and press their economic demands.
A farmers' committee met Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas and Simitis's special envoy George Paschalidis but came away empty handed.
"The prime minister has rejected our demands. Our struggle will go on and intensify," Yannis Pattakis, a farmers' leader, said after leaving the meeting in parliament.
More than 7,000 farmers erupted in boos, insults and chants against the socialist government's 1997 budget, which was being debated inside the parliament.
"Fight, farmers fight. They are sucking our blood," chanted more than 7,000 farmers gathered outside parliament.
The farmers have blocked roads for 22 days with tractors, causing transport chaos and inflicting more than $100 million in damages on the economy.
They want lower fuel prices, higher price supports and $1.3 billion in debts rescheduled but Simitis has said the state has no more money to give to farmers or anyone else.
The rally was one of the largest so far in a campaign by an array of groups -- including public workers, seamen, teachers, pensioners and farmers -- against Simitis's reform policies.
Seamen set a new 24-hour strike for Friday after stopping many ships from docking on Thursday and clashing with police at several ports.
The Panhellenic Seamen's Federation (PNO) said it extended the strike, which began on Monday, to protest against rising unemployment and the abolition of special tax exemptions.
Police said there were clashes at the ports of Piraeus, near Athens, and Patras in western Greece.
Seaman have been stopping most ships from docking, often by diving into the sea in front of piers. They have had fist fights with lorry drivers trying to unload goods.
The clashes on Wednesday and Thursday involved both seamen and police, and seamen and drivers.
In recent days many of the farmers' barricades have come down but blockades on the north-south motorway in the Thessaly region have stayed in place, virtually cutting Greece in two.
Farmers have called repeatedly for direct talks with Simitis but he slammed the door on them again on Thursday, refusing to meet directly while roads were blocked.
In an interview published on Thursday in Nitro magazine, Simitis stood by his rejection of concessions for farmers or other workers who have staged protests.

"I'd rather go home (quit)," he said when asked if he would yield to protesters. "My job is to spread the existing money in a socially just way and that is why we must fight not to succumb to blackmail."
In neighbouring Albania, customs officials said around 150 trucks left for Greece on Thursday, hoping to use country routes to get around main roads which have been blocked with tractors.
The farmers' blockade is hurting Albania, Europe's poorest country, and has forced several factories to shut down. Prices have jumped 20 percent in the main southern town of Gjirokaster.
"Our patience has run out, we can't wait any longer. Our market needs the goods so badly," Altin Doko, a trader in the main Gjirokaster market, told Reuters.
